hero.heading:
What is
a SPACT?
hero.standfirst: A SPACT is a Special Action supporting artist: a background performer booked for a real, proven skill (fighting, riding, dancing, driving, drilling like a soldier) and engaged to perform that skill safely and repeatably on camera.
hero.imageAlt: Storyboard frame of a crowd scene with six SPACTs marked out by callout boxes

origin.heading: Where the word comes from

paragraph1.after: . On UK productions, supporting artists are engaged on crowd agreements, and when a role calls for genuine physical ability the booking is designated special action, a SPACT for short. The term lives in call sheets, crowd budgets and AD department shorthand rather than in any glossary, which is why so few people outside a set have heard it.

origin.paragraph2: In practice, you'll hear it used as a noun for the performer themselves: "we need six SPACTs for the fight in the market", "the riders are SPACTs, not doubles". It signals to everyone on set (ADs, stunt coordinators, HODs) that the person can genuinely do the thing the scene requires, and has been booked, briefed and paid accordingly.

seeFrame.heading: SPACT, stunt performer, supporting artist
seeFrame.body: The three roles sit on one spectrum of screen action, and the fastest way to see where the lines fall is to look at a single shot with all three marked out on it. That comparison lives on our SPACTs page: pick a role, or click a performer in the frame, and it isolates them.

work.heading: What SPACTs are booked to do
work.intro: Anywhere a scene needs genuine ability in the background rather than a mime of it. Typical bookings we supply:

rows.description: Background brawls, battle lines, gunmen in shootouts: choreographed contact that reads as real.
Ballroom, Latin, club and period social dance filling a floor with people who can actually dance it.
Ex-forces performers who move, drill and handle weapons the way the real thing does.
Horse riders, cyclists and precision drivers working around principal action.
Gymnasts, acrobats, circus and creature performers: anywhere physical control is the skill.

practice.heading: Where SPACTs actually get used
practice.intro: The same booking turns up again and again across four kinds of production. These are the briefs that land on our desk most often.

cases.title: Battles, sieges and army scenes
cases.body: Period and fantasy drama fills the frame with soldiers, and the shield lines, sword work and cavalry all have to read as real from the second row back. SPACTs carry that action for days on end while the stunt team handles the falls and the fire.

cases.title: Crowds, uprisings and creature work
cases.body: Riot lines, marching troopers and performers inside creature suits or heavy prosthetics: physical control is the skill, and it has to survive take after take under lights.

cases.title: Police, military and medical procedure
cases.body: Ex-forces and serving-trained performers who hold a weapon, clear a room or work a scene the way the real thing does, so nothing on screen contradicts the story.

cases.title: Campaigns that have to be done for real
cases.body: Car films needing a driver who can perform rather than pose, sportswear shoots wanting genuine free-runners, gymnasts and dancers, and cinematic spots calling for fight or aerial work.

booking.heading: How SPACTs are booked, and what to expect
paragraphs: SPACTs are booked through the crowd department, usually via an agency that specialises in them. The production sends a brief (the skill, the level, the look, the dates) and the agency returns a book of artists it can vouch for. Assessed skill levels matter more than showreels here: on the day, the performer either can or cannot do what the scene needs.

A production should expect a SPACT to arrive set-ready: briefed on the action, able to repeat it take after take, comfortable taking direction from ADs and coordinators, and clear about their own limits. Rates sit above standard background rates, agreed per the crowd agreement in place, with the special action noted on the chit.
Every SPACT on our books has been assessed and interviewed by the Take 3 team before joining. When we send someone to set, they are exactly who we say they are.
